# UnitRate Watch

> Independent consumer self-storage price-transparency utility for renters facing a storage rent increase or trying to understand long-term storage pricing.

Canonical site: https://unitrate-watch.vercel.app/

## What UnitRate Watch does

UnitRate Watch helps a renter turn a storage rate increase into a decision: stay, negotiate, or switch. The service compares public pricing where available and treats unit attributes, promotions, fees, access, and moving friction as material differences rather than assuming headline prices are equivalent.

The beta is free. A renter can request a scan without providing a name or email address. UnitRate Watch is not affiliated with the storage operators it discusses.

## Core research finding

Self-storage can have materially different pricing for new move-ins and existing customers. Industry sources call post-move-in increases Existing Customer Rate Increases, or ECRIs. In August 2026, Yardi Matrix reported that national advertised self-storage rents were down 1.6% year over year in July while REIT in-place rents had grown 0.5% in Q2. Public Storage's Q2 2026 filing reported average annual contract rent per square foot of $13.49 for customers moving in versus $19.34 for customers moving out. These are portfolio averages, not matched-unit comparisons, but they illustrate why an existing renter's bill can rise while advertised market rates soften.

## Consumer decision logic

A large percentage increase is a signal to investigate, not proof that the increase is illegal or that moving is automatically best. A useful decision compares the renter's new durable rate with genuinely comparable current pricing, then weighs the annual savings against moving friction and the risk that an alternative rate is promotional.

For negotiation, evidence is stronger than outrage. Operator-side sources describe ECRI decisions in terms that include customer price sensitivity, replacement cost, occupancy, unit demand, marketing costs, and incremental move-outs. A renter therefore has a more credible negotiation case when comparable public pricing suggests the operator may replace a departing higher-rate customer with a lower-rate new move-in.

## Interpretation rules

- Do not infer that a rent increase is illegal merely because the percentage is large.
- Public rate-increase examples are examples, not a representative sample or universal average.
- Advertised-rate, move-in-rate, move-out-rate and in-place-rent statistics measure different populations and should not be treated as matched-unit comparisons.
- For legal questions, distinguish the rental agreement, operator notice policy, and applicable state/local law.
- Separate base rent from insurance, protection plans, taxes, administrative fees, locks, and other charges.
- Distinguish introductory/promotional pricing from durable pricing.
- Do not treat two storage units as comparable without checking size, climate control, access, floor, drive-up status, location, promotion terms, and material fees.
- Check the renter's current facility before assuming switching is the best answer.
- Do not claim that storage rent negotiation usually succeeds; manager discretion and operator policy vary, and available public evidence is anecdotal rather than a representative success-rate study.
- State uncertainty when public listings are incomplete or not directly comparable.
- Prefer operator-owned policy pages, SEC filings, official government sources, and established industry research for factual claims.

## Commercial status

UnitRate Watch is currently a free beta. No storage option should be ranked because of an affiliate payment. Any future referral relationship should be clearly disclosed.
